name: Failed Physics Bets
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Not Every Bet Pays Off: When Physics Promises Fall Short
lesson.summary: GPS and MRI show that patient physics research can pay off enormously, but the same optimism that funded them has also funded expensive dead ends and outright deceptions, and a skeptic needs practice telling the difference in advance.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters told a flattering story. Fund basic, curiosity-driven physics research into atomic transitions or nuclear spin, wait a few decades, and you might end up with GPS or MRI, technologies that quietly underpin modern life. That story is true, but told on its own it invites a kind of survivorship bias. For every research program that eventually became GPS or MRI, there have been others that consumed comparable money, talent, and public excitement, and simply did not deliver.

It helps to notice that failure comes in more than one flavor, because they call for different reactions from a skeptical reader. Sometimes the underlying science is basically sound and the technology genuinely works, but the economics never add up, the thing is real but not worth what it cost, which is the story the Concorde chapter will tell. Sometimes a research team announces a striking result that later turns out not to replicate under independent scrutiny, without anyone necessarily lying, which is the story of cold fusion. And sometimes a technology is deliberately misrepresented to investors, regulators, or the public by people who knew, or should have known, that it did not work as claimed, which is the story of Theranos.

That third category deserves a different kind of judgment than the first two. Chasing a real hypothesis that turns out to be wrong is normal science, and punishing it too harshly would discourage exactly the kind of risk-taking that produced GPS and MRI in the first place. But when overpromising crosses into deliberately misleading people who are relying on your representations to make decisions with their money or their health, that is not a bad bet anymore, it is a different problem, and it deserves a different response.

The next few chapters walk through cold fusion, Theranos, and the Concorde in that order, three real, well-documented case studies that each illustrate a different way an ambitious technology promise can go wrong: an honest scientific error made worse by skipping normal verification, a fraud built on a gap between what a founder claimed and what she knew, and a technically successful machine that was never going to make economic sense. After that, the book turns to the broader pattern connecting these stories, why charismatic founders in particular tend to attract this kind of trouble, and how a careful reader can learn to recognize, in advance, when a scientist or a founder is misleading their backers or the public. All of this groundwork exists for a reason: the final chapters of this unit turn the same scrutiny on quantum computing itself, and a reader who has practiced spotting the warning signs in these historical cases will be far better equipped to evaluate quantum computing claims on their own merits.
